title: How LLMs Work
tagline: Large language models predict the next token — and from that single objective, language understanding emerges.

sections.content:
Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini are neural networks trained to predict what token comes next in a sequence. From this deceptively simple objective — trained on trillions of tokens of text — they develop the ability to reason, write code, translate languages, and follow complex instructions.

Understanding LLMs requires four concepts: **tokens** (how text is broken into chunks), **embeddings** (how tokens become vectors), the **Transformer architecture** (how context is processed via attention), and the **training vs inference** distinction (what happens before and after deployment). The **context window** determines how much the model can 'see' at once — a fundamental constraint that shapes how you build applications on top of LLMs.

sections.title: An Extremely Well-Read Autocomplete
sections.content:
Your phone's autocomplete suggests the next word based on the words you just typed. An LLM is conceptually the same — but trained on almost the entire internet rather than your text messages, and with 100 billion+ parameters instead of a simple lookup table.

The critical difference is **attention**: your phone's autocomplete looks at only the last few words. An LLM's attention mechanism looks at every single token in the context simultaneously and learns to selectively focus — when completing 'The Eiffel Tower is in...', attention routes focus toward 'Eiffel Tower' and its strong association with 'Paris', even if hundreds of tokens separate them. This parallel, global context awareness is what makes LLMs qualitatively different from earlier sequential models.

**Tokens** are the atomic units of text an LLM processes. Tokenisers (such as Byte-Pair Encoding, BPE) split text into subword chunks: 'unhappiness' might become `['un', 'happ', 'iness']`, each mapped to an integer ID. Common words are single tokens; rare words split into multiple tokens. A rough rule of thumb: 1 token ≈ 0.75 English words (GPT-4o tokenises 'Hello, world!' as 4 tokens). Token count matters for cost and context window limits.

**Embeddings** convert integer token IDs into dense floating-point vectors (typically 768–12,288 dimensions). These vectors are learned during training so that tokens with related meanings cluster nearby in vector space — 'king' and 'queen' are geometrically close. Positional encodings are added to the embeddings so the model knows token order, since attention itself is position-agnostic.

**The Transformer and attention** are the architectural core. A Transformer processes the entire token sequence in parallel through multiple layers. Each layer contains:
- **Multi-head self-attention**: every token attends to every other token, computing how much each position should inform the current position's representation. Multiple 'heads' run in parallel, each attending to different relationship patterns.
- **Feed-forward network**: a two-layer MLP applied independently to each position after attention, adding representational capacity.
- **Layer normalisation + residual connections**: stabilise training and allow gradients to flow through many layers.

A GPT-style (decoder-only) model generates text autoregressively: given a prefix, it predicts the next token, appends it to the context, then predicts the next, and so on. **Causal masking** ensures each token attends only to previous tokens during training, preventing the model from 'cheating' by looking at future tokens.

**Training vs inference**: during training, the model sees trillions of text tokens, and for each position predicts the next token — cross-entropy loss penalises wrong predictions, gradients flow back, and weights update. This can take months on thousands of GPUs. During **inference**, weights are frozen. A user's prompt is tokenised, processed in a single forward pass (for the full prompt), and then new tokens are generated one at a time. Inference is cheap relative to training — the same trained weights serve millions of users.

**Context window** is the maximum number of tokens the model can process in one forward pass. GPT-4 supports 128k tokens; Claude 3.5 Sonnet supports 200k tokens. Everything outside the context window is invisible to the model. Long contexts increase memory and compute quadratically with attention (O(n²) in naive attention), which is why efficient attention variants (FlashAttention, sparse attention) are important for long-context models.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The tokenisation demo shows how text maps to integer IDs — real models use learned BPE merges that split unknown words into known subword pieces. The attention demo implements scaled dot-product attention for three toy tokens: query[0] has a high dot product with key[0], so weights[0] is high and the output blends mostly values[0]. The sqrt(d_k) scaling prevents dot products from growing too large and pushing softmax into saturation. Token counting is essential for staying within context windows and estimating API costs.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **The context window is the model's working memory.** Everything the model 'knows about your conversation' must fit inside it. When building LLM applications, track token counts carefully — truncated context causes the model to forget earlier instructions or conversation history silently. For long documents, use techniques like **RAG** (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) to retrieve only the relevant chunks rather than stuffing everything into the context. The KV-cache also means that re-sending the same system prompt at the start of each request can be cached and is much cheaper than it appears.

items: **Tokens** are subword text units (~0.75 words each). LLMs process token IDs, not raw characters. Token count determines cost, speed, and whether content fits in the context window.
**Embeddings** map token IDs to dense vectors where semantic similarity is encoded geometrically. Positional encodings are added so the model knows token order.

**Self-attention** allows every token to attend to every other token in the context, computing a weighted mixture of all positions. This is what gives Transformers their powerful long-range context awareness.

**Training** is expensive (months, thousands of GPUs, next-token prediction on trillions of tokens). **Inference** uses frozen weights and generates one token at a time autoregressively — vastly cheaper.

**Context window** is the hard limit on tokens per forward pass. Exceeding it silently truncates context. Efficient use of the context window (RAG, KV-caching, careful prompting) is central to production LLM engineering.

quiz.question: What is the primary training objective of a GPT-style large language model?
options: Predicting whether a sentence is grammatically correct
Predicting the next token given all previous tokens in the sequence
Classifying text into predefined categories
Translating text between languages
quiz.explanation: GPT-style models are trained with a next-token prediction (causal language modelling) objective. Given all previous tokens, predict the next one. This single objective — applied at massive scale — causes the model to develop broad language understanding as an emergent capability.

quiz.question: Approximately how many English words does 1 token correspond to on average?
options: 3 words
1 word
0.75 words
4 words
quiz.explanation: As a rough rule of thumb, 1 token ≈ 0.75 English words, or equivalently, ~1.33 tokens per word. Short common words are single tokens; longer or rarer words split into multiple tokens. This affects cost estimation and context window planning when building LLM applications.

quiz.question: What does the self-attention mechanism compute for each token?
options: The token's character-level spelling
A weighted sum of all other tokens' value vectors, where weights reflect relevance
The grammatical part of speech of the token
A random sample from the token's embedding
quiz.explanation: Self-attention computes attention scores between a query (current token) and all keys (all tokens), applies softmax to get weights, then computes a weighted sum of value vectors. This allows each token to gather information from any other token in the context, regardless of distance.

quiz.question: Why is logit scaling by sqrt(d_k) applied before softmax in attention?
options: To normalise the attention weights to sum to 1
To prevent dot products from growing large and pushing softmax into saturation, which causes vanishing gradients
To convert the logits into token probabilities
To apply positional information to the attention scores
quiz.explanation: For large embedding dimensions d_k, dot products grow in magnitude proportionally to sqrt(d_k). Large logits push softmax toward a one-hot distribution, causing near-zero gradients for all non-maximum positions — effectively freezing most of the attention weights. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps logits in a stable range.

quiz.question: What is a context window in an LLM?
options: A sliding window that caches recent conversations between sessions
The maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single forward pass
The number of transformer layers in the model
The temperature range used during sampling
quiz.explanation: The context window is the hard upper limit on tokens per inference call. Content beyond the window is invisible — the model cannot attend to it. GPT-4o supports 128k tokens; Claude 3.5 Sonnet supports 200k. Exceeding the limit requires techniques like truncation, summarisation, or RAG.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between LLM training and inference?
options: Training uses attention; inference does not
Training updates model weights via backprop on massive data; inference uses frozen weights to generate tokens one at a time
Inference requires more compute than training
Training processes one token at a time; inference processes all tokens in parallel
quiz.explanation: Training adjusts billions of parameters via backpropagation over trillions of tokens — a massive one-time cost. Inference uses those frozen weights: the full prompt is processed in parallel (one forward pass), then new tokens are generated autoregressively one-at-a-time. The same weights serve all users.

quiz.question: What is the KV-cache in LLM inference?
options: A database of common knowledge injected into the model at startup
Cached Key and Value matrices from previous tokens, avoiding recomputation on each new generation step
A key-value store for storing conversation history between sessions
The vocabulary lookup table mapping token IDs to embeddings
quiz.explanation: During autoregressive generation, each new token needs attention over all previous tokens. Without caching, all Key and Value matrices would be recomputed from scratch each step — O(n²) cost per token. The KV-cache stores previously computed K and V tensors so only the new token's K/V are computed, dramatically speeding up generation.

quiz.question: What does a low temperature setting (e.g., temperature=0) do to LLM output?
options: Causes the model to refuse to generate output
Increases randomness and creativity in generation
Makes the model always select the highest-probability token (greedy decoding), producing deterministic output
Reduces the context window to save memory
quiz.explanation: Temperature scales logits before softmax. Low temperature sharpens the distribution toward the highest-probability token. At temperature=0, this is greedy decoding — the model always picks the single most likely next token, producing deterministic and typically factual but potentially repetitive output. High temperature flattens the distribution, increasing variety and creativity.

quiz.question: What is RLHF and why is it used to train LLMs?
options: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — fine-tunes models to be helpful, harmless, and follow instructions using human preference rankings
Recursive Layer-wise Hierarchical Fine-tuning — speeds up training by fine-tuning layers independently
Retrieval-augmented Learning with Human Feedback — injects web search results into training
Regularised Language Hyperparameter Fine-tuning — optimises learning rate schedules
quiz.explanation: RLHF aligns LLMs with human preferences. Human raters rank model outputs for quality; a reward model is trained on these rankings; the LLM is then fine-tuned using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimisation) to maximise the reward model's score. This is why ChatGPT-style models follow instructions better than raw pretrained models.

quiz.question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and when is it used?
options: A training technique that retrieves similar documents and augments the training loss
A technique that retrieves relevant documents at inference time and injects them into the prompt, allowing the model to answer questions beyond its training cutoff or context limit
A method to increase the context window by compressing the KV-cache
A hardware optimisation that retrieves weights from a faster memory tier
quiz.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant document chunks (typically via embedding similarity search) and inserts them into the LLM prompt. This allows the model to answer questions using up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge not in its training data, without retraining. It is the standard approach for building Q&A systems over private or frequently changing document collections.
